passage:
Friday evening: Lakshmi told Omkar about tomorrow's zoo trip. He flapped his hands, bounced on the bed and squealed until bedtime.
Saturday: he bounced in his seat the whole way there and shrieked at the elephants.
Sunday morning: when Lakshmi said, "No zoo today," Omkar burst into tears and lay face down on the floor.
"Next time," Lakshmi told her husband, "we'll tell him on the morning, not the night before."

qa.q: What did Omkar shriek at on Saturday?
qa.a: The elephants.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling on Sunday when he burst into tears?
qa.a: He was disappointed and let down after two days of excitement, and may also have been tired from the trip.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi decide to change next time?
qa.a: To tell him about a trip only on the morning, so the build-up is smaller.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi's husband see the Sunday tears?
qa.a: He might see them as a strange overreaction until Lakshmi links them to the big build-up.

grounding: Over a weekend a toddler's bouncing, squealing excitement about the zoo turns to tears when it ends.

passage:
The kulfi cart's bell rang in the Kolkata lane. Saurabh flapped both hands and bounced, squealing, pulling at his uncle Deepak's kurta. Deepak laughed and bounced with him, and soon they were both hopping at the window.
The kulfi was cold and sweet. But when the last bit slid off the stick, Saurabh's face crumpled and he wailed.
Deepak scooped him up. "All gone. That was so exciting, and now it's finished. I know."

qa.q: What rang in the lane?
qa.a: The kulfi cart's bell.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling when the last bit slid off the stick?
qa.a: He was disappointed and sad that the treat was over, after all that excitement.

qa.q: What did Deepak do that helped when the tears came?
qa.a: He picked Saurabh up and named both the excitement and the ending, offering comfort.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel when Saurabh bounced at the window?
qa.a: Deepak caught the excitement and felt playful, bouncing along with him. 😊

grounding: A toddler's contagious excitement about a treat turns to tears when it ends, and his uncle comforts him.

passage:
"Nana's coming! Nana's coming!" Urmila squealed, bouncing at the window.
"She's been like this for an hour," said her mother.
"Don't wind her up more, Harsha," she warned her husband.
"Car! Car!" Harsha shouted, and Urmila shrieked, flapping her hands.
But when Nana walked in, Urmila hid behind the curtain and started to cry.
"Too much build-up," said her mother. Harsha picked her up gently. "It's okay. Nana will wait."

qa.q: Where did Urmila hide when Nana walked in?
qa.a: Behind the curtain.

qa.q: Why did Urmila cry when Nana finally arrived?
qa.a: After an hour of excitement she was probably overwhelmed, and the big moment tipped into tears.

qa.q: What could the family try next time a visitor is coming?
qa.a: Keep the build-up calmer and shorter, rather than winding her up for an hour.

qa.q: How might Nana feel when Urmila hides and cries?
qa.a: Nana might feel a little hurt, but understand that Urmila was overwhelmed.

grounding: A toddler bounces and squeals for an hour waiting for her grandfather, and the big build-up turns to tears.

passage:
Monday: at a party, a popper went bang. Afreen startled and looked at Zubin, her father. He had jumped too, face worried. Afreen burst into tears.
Wednesday: a balloon popped at home. Zubin laughed calmly. "Pop!" Afreen startled, looked at him, then laughed.
The next Monday: Afreen squeezed a bubble and it popped. She gasped, eyes wide, looked at Zubin, and giggled.

qa.q: What popped on Wednesday?
qa.a: A balloon.

qa.q: Why did Afreen cry on Monday but laugh on Wednesday?
qa.a: On Monday she saw her father's worried face and felt frightened; on Wednesday his calm laugh made the surprise feel safe and funny.

qa.q: What did Zubin learn over the week?
qa.a: That his calm reaction helps Afreen turn a surprise into laughter instead of fear.

qa.q: How might Zubin feel the next Monday?
qa.a: He would likely feel pleased and relieved that Afreen now finds surprises fun.

grounding: Over a week a father learns his calm reaction turns his toddler's surprise into laughter rather than fear.

passage:
Dolma from next door handed Bhupen a round tin in their Guwahati flat. "Open it."
He pulled the lid, and a cloth snake sprang out. Bhupen gasped, eyes huge, and dropped the tin. He froze, looking at Dolma's face.
Dolma smiled wide. "Surprise! A silly snake!" Bhupen let out a shaky laugh, then a real one, and pushed the snake back in to try again.

qa.q: What sprang out of the tin?
qa.a: A cloth snake.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling when he froze and looked at Dolma?
qa.a: He was surprised and unsure whether to be scared; her smile made him feel safe, so he laughed.

qa.q: What did Dolma do that helped Bhupen?
qa.a: She smiled and named it a silly surprise, showing it was safe.

qa.q: What would change if Dolma had shrieked too?
qa.a: Bhupen would likely have read it as danger and cried instead of laughing.

grounding: A toddler gasps at a pop-up toy and checks a neighbour's face, whose calm smile turns surprise into laughter.

passage:
"Cuckoo! Cuckoo!" The little bird shot out of the clock.
Ishita gasped and froze, eyes wide, spoon halfway to her mouth.
"Is she scared?" asked her mother.
"Cuckoo says hello, Ishita!" said Neelam, her Nani, calmly waving at it.
Ishita looked at Nani, then at the clock. The bird popped back in. She laughed and pointed.
"Again?"
"Next hour," said Nani, smiling.

qa.q: What shot out of the clock?
qa.a: A little bird.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling when she froze?
qa.a: She was surprised and unsure, checking Nani's face to see if it was safe; Nani's calm made her laugh.

qa.q: What did Neelam do that helped?
qa.a: She stayed calm and made the bird friendly by saying it was saying hello and waving.

qa.q: How does Ishita's mother first read the gasp?
qa.a: She wonders if Ishita is scared.

grounding: A toddler freezes in surprise at a cuckoo clock, and her grandmother's calm reaction turns it into laughter.

passage:
It was late at the temple fair. Jeevan had missed his afternoon nap. He whined, rubbed his eyes and clung to Pranav's leg. When Pranav said no to a plastic whistle, Jeevan threw himself on the ground, screaming.
"Spoilt boy," muttered a relative.
"He's not spoilt, he's worn out," said Pranav, lifting him. By the time they reached the road home, Jeevan was asleep on his shoulder.

qa.q: What had Jeevan missed?
qa.a: His afternoon nap.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling when he threw himself on the ground?
qa.a: He was overtired and frustrated, not simply spoilt.

qa.q: Which of Pranav's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: Reading the meltdown as tiredness and carrying him home worked, because sleep was what he needed.

qa.q: How does the relative see Jeevan's meltdown?
qa.a: The relative sees it as spoilt behaviour, not tiredness.

grounding: A father reads his toddler's meltdown at a late fair as tiredness, not naughtiness, and lets him sleep.

passage:
After a long day at the beach in São Paulo, Priscila threw her cup on the floor. "No! Red one!" She whined, clung to her mother's leg, then collapsed into sobs.
"Such a naughty girl today," said Ulla, her grandmother.
"She's exhausted," said her mother. "Bath and bed." Twenty minutes later, Priscila was asleep, her cheeks still pink from the sun.

qa.q: What colour cup did Priscila want?
qa.a: Red.

qa.q: What was Priscila feeling when she collapsed into sobs?
qa.a: She was exhausted after a long beach day, which made small upsets feel huge.

qa.q: What did Priscila's mother do that fixed it?
qa.a: She read the meltdown as tiredness and gave her a bath and bed.

qa.q: How does Ulla see Priscila's behaviour?
qa.a: Ulla sees it as naughtiness, not tiredness.

grounding: A mother reads her toddler's meltdown after a long day as exhaustion, and rest fixes it.

passage: I'm Wasim, from the fourth floor. At seven on Monday evening, the lift doors opened and there was little Ojas, screaming and kicking on the floor, whining that he wanted to press the button. His mother didn't shout. She picked him up and said softly, "Too tired." The next morning, same lift, Ojas pressed the button for me, cheerful as anything. I think he just needed his sleep.

qa.q: What did Ojas want to press?
qa.a: The lift button.

qa.q: What might Ojas have been feeling on Monday evening?
qa.a: He was probably overtired, which made him frustrated and upset over something small.

qa.q: What did the mother's calm response show about the meltdown?
qa.a: That she read it as tiredness and helped him rest instead of scolding.

qa.q: How does Wasim see Ojas by the next morning?
qa.a: Wasim sees a cheerful boy and realises Monday's scene was about tiredness.

grounding: A neighbour sees a toddler's evening meltdown and cheerful morning, and realises tiredness was the cause.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage:
Monday: Nani arrived. Minakshi jumped and squealed, then burst into tears while still hugging her. Dilnaz checked: no bump, no hunger. "Too much happy," she said, and held her.
Wednesday evening: tears again, with eye-rubbing and yawns. Dilnaz took her to bed.
Friday: tears while holding her tummy before lunch. Dilnaz fed her, and the tears stopped.

qa.q: What did Minakshi do when Nani arrived?
qa.a: She jumped and squealed, then burst into tears while still hugging her.

qa.q: What was Minakshi feeling behind Monday's tears?
qa.a: She was overwhelmed with joy at seeing Nani, a kind of happy overload rather than pain or sadness.

qa.q: What habit helped Dilnaz understand each lot of tears?
qa.a: She checked Minakshi's body and the setting each time before deciding what the tears meant.

qa.q: How might Nani feel when Minakshi cries while hugging her?
qa.a: Nani might feel surprised or unsure at first, then touched once she understands it was joy.

grounding: Over a week a mother checks body and setting to read her toddler's tears as joy overload, tiredness or hunger.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage:
At the birthday party in Pune, the magician pulled a rabbit from his hat. Anirban clapped, laughed and suddenly burst into tears, still clapping.
Uday, his father, checked him over. No bump. He had eaten. It wasn't sleep time.
"Too exciting?" Uday asked, lifting him. Anirban sobbed and giggled at the same time. Uday carried him out to the balcony for a few quiet minutes, and he calmed.

qa.q: What did the magician pull from his hat?
qa.a: A rabbit.

qa.q: What was Anirban feeling when he burst into tears while clapping?
qa.a: He was overwhelmed by excitement and joy, which spilled over into tears.

qa.q: What did Uday do that helped?
qa.a: He checked for pain, hunger and tiredness, then gave Anirban a quiet break from the excitement.

qa.q: How might the magician see Anirban's tears?
qa.a: The magician might worry the trick frightened him, not knowing it was joy overload.

grounding: A father checks his toddler's body and setting and reads tears at a magic show as joy overload.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage:
"Why is she crying? I only gave her the new doll!" said Siddharth, Zainab's uncle.
"Maybe she doesn't like it?"
"She's holding it tight."
Zainab's mother knelt and looked her over. "Her foot. Look." Zainab's toe was caught in the strap of her sandal, bent back.
She freed it gently and rubbed it. Zainab's tears slowed. She hugged the doll.
"So not the doll at all," Siddharth said.

qa.q: What was caught in Zainab's sandal strap?
qa.a: Her toe.

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling while she cried?
qa.a: She was in pain from her toe being bent back, not unhappy with the doll.

qa.q: What did Zainab's mother do that found the real reason?
qa.a: She checked Zainab's body instead of guessing from the moment.

qa.q: How does Siddharth feel at first when Zainab cries?
qa.a: He feels worried and a bit hurt that she might not like his gift.

grounding: A mother checks her toddler's body and finds pain, not the new doll, behind her tears.

passage:
In the village courtyard, Hrithik spilled his milk and screamed, stamping. His grandmother, Maria, pointed. "Look, the rooster!" Within a minute, he was giggling at it.
But that afternoon he whined and fussed for hours, pulled at his ear and wouldn't eat. No rooster helped. Maria felt his forehead. Warm. She took him to the doctor that evening.

qa.q: What did Maria point at?
qa.a: The rooster.

qa.q: What was Hrithik likely feeling during the long afternoon of fussing?
qa.a: He was likely unwell and uncomfortable, which is why distraction didn't help like it did in the morning.

qa.q: What told Maria the afternoon was different from the morning?
qa.a: The fussing lasted for hours, he pulled at his ear and wouldn't eat, and his forehead was warm.

qa.q: What would change if Maria had kept trying to distract him?
qa.a: A possible illness might have gone unchecked, and Hrithik would have stayed uncomfortable.

grounding: A grandmother sees her toddler's brief tantrum pass with distraction and his long fussing signal a health need.

passage:
The lift doors closed before Oskar could press the button, there in the lobby of their Oslo building. He screamed and threw himself against Lindiwe's legs.
"Oh, look!" Lindiwe pointed at the window. "A magpie!"
Oskar stopped mid-scream and looked. The bird hopped along the railing. A giggle burst out of him.
By the time the lift came back, he was pressing the button, beaming.

qa.q: What bird did Lindiwe point at?
qa.a: A magpie.

qa.q: What was Oskar feeling when he screamed at the lift doors?
qa.a: He was frustrated at missing his turn to press the button, but the feeling passed quickly.

qa.q: Why did distraction work here?
qa.a: Because it was a short burst of frustration with no deeper need behind it.

qa.q: How might Lindiwe feel when Oskar giggles?
qa.a: She probably feels amused and relieved at how fast his mood switched.

grounding: A toddler's brief frustration flips to giggles with distraction, showing how fast short displays pass.

passage: I'm Pema, and I live next door to Farhan's family. On Saturday I saw him wail in the shop because his mother wouldn't buy sweets. A minute later a cat walked in, and he was laughing. On Tuesday, though, he fussed and cried all afternoon, and nothing worked. His mother realised lunch had been skipped in the rush. After a meal he was fine. I learned the long ones mean something.

qa.q: What walked into the shop?
qa.a: A cat.

qa.q: What was Farhan likely feeling during the long fussing on Tuesday?
qa.a: He was hungry and cranky because he had missed his lunch.

qa.q: What should adults do when a toddler's upset lasts a long time?
qa.a: Look for a need underneath, such as hunger, tiredness or illness, as Farhan's mother did.

qa.q: How does Pema see the difference between the two days?
qa.a: Pema sees that short outbursts pass quickly, while long ones point to a real need.

grounding: A neighbour sees a toddler's brief outburst pass with distraction and a lasting one reveal hunger.

passage:
The goat sneezed in the village yard, and Suraj burst out laughing, a real belly laugh.
Later, when his sister Ishita turned to chat with a neighbour, Suraj started to cry loudly, "Waaah!" But there were no tears, and he peeked between his fingers to see if she was looking.
Ishita didn't scold. She knelt beside him. "You want me to play with you?" Suraj nodded, and the crying stopped.

qa.q: What made Suraj laugh?
qa.a: The goat sneezed.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling when he fake-cried?
qa.a: He felt left out and wanted his sister's attention, so he used a deliberate cry to get it.

qa.q: Which of Ishita's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: Responding to the need, asking if he wanted to play, worked, because it met his wish for attention without shaming him.

qa.q: How might the neighbour see Suraj's crying?
qa.a: The neighbour might find it funny, noticing the peeking and no tears.

grounding: A toddler laughs spontaneously and later fake-cries for attention, and his sister responds to the need underneath.

passage:
In their Copenhagen kitchen, Soo-ah was on a long phone call. Anders, on the floor, started to make crying noises. "Wah, wah." No tears. He watched her the whole time.
Soo-ah said goodbye and hung up. She sat beside him. "You wanted me. I'm here now."
Anders grinned and handed her a block. Earlier, when the cat had sneezed, his laugh had been real and sudden. This one was different, planned. But the need was real too.

qa.q: What did Anders hand Soo-ah?
qa.a: A block.

qa.q: What was Anders feeling when he made crying noises with no tears?
qa.a: He felt ignored during the long call and wanted his mother's attention.

qa.q: What did Soo-ah do that was wise?
qa.a: She responded to the real need for attention rather than scolding the fake cry.

qa.q: How might Soo-ah see the fake cry?
qa.a: She sees it as a sign that Anders is learning to use a display on purpose, and that he needs her.

grounding: A mother notices her toddler's fake cry is deliberate and responds to his need for attention.

passage: I'm Yamini, Deepika's aunt. When the family gathered to see the new baby cousin, Deepika sat quiet for a while. Then she started to cry, loud, but with no tears, peeking at us all through her fingers. Earlier she'd laughed properly at the baby's hiccups. Her mother didn't tell her off. She lifted Deepika onto her lap and said, "You want a cuddle too." Deepika snuggled in and stopped at once.

qa.q: What had Deepika laughed at earlier?
qa.a: The baby's hiccups.

qa.q: What might Deepika have been feeling when she fake-cried?
qa.a: She was probably feeling left out while everyone looked at the new baby and wanted attention too.

qa.q: What did Deepika's mother do that met the real need?
qa.a: She lifted her onto her lap and named her wish for a cuddle, without scolding.

qa.q: How does Yamini see Deepika's crying?
qa.a: Yamini notices the cry is put on but also sees the real feeling underneath.

grounding: An aunt sees a toddler fake-cry for attention when a new baby arrives, and her mother responds to the need.

passage:
Manjula tripped over a root in the village yard and fell flat. She wailed. Pema, the neighbour, ran over and picked her up, rocking her. Manjula looked up at her, sobbing, and then smiled, a wobbly smile through the tears.
"See, she's fine, she's smiling," called someone.
Pema kept holding her. "Still crying, though." She rocked her until the sobs stopped completely.

qa.q: What did Manjula trip over?
qa.a: A root in the village yard.

qa.q: What did Manjula's wobbly smile through tears show?
qa.a: It showed relief at being comforted, mixed with the pain and fright of the fall.

qa.q: Why did Pema keep holding Manjula?
qa.a: Because Manjula was still crying, and comfort should follow the crying, not the smile.

qa.q: How does the person calling out read the smile?
qa.a: They take the smile as a sign she's fine and no longer needs comfort.

grounding: A neighbour keeps comforting a toddler who smiles through her tears after a fall, following the crying rather than the smile.

passage:
Marek tumbled off his scooter in the Warsaw park and scraped his knee. He screamed. Lucia, his mother, knelt and blew on the scrape. Marek looked at her, still sobbing, and gave a small, teary smile.
"There, he's fine," said his uncle. "Put him down."
"He's still crying," Lucia said. She held him close until his breathing steadied. Only then did she set him back on the scooter.

qa.q: What did Marek scrape?
qa.a: His knee.

qa.q: What was Marek feeling when he smiled through his sobs?
qa.a: He was relieved to be comforted, while still hurting and upset from the fall.

qa.q: Which of Lucia's choices was wise, and why?
qa.a: Holding him until his breathing steadied was wise, because the smile didn't mean the distress had passed.

qa.q: How does Marek's uncle read the smile?
qa.a: The uncle takes it to mean Marek is fine, missing that he is still crying.

grounding: A mother keeps comforting her toddler who smiles through tears after a fall, following the crying not the smile.

passage: I'm Wasim, and I was having tea with Payal's family when she bumped her head on the table. She screamed. Her father held her, and when he made a silly face, she smiled at him, but tears were still pouring down. He didn't stop holding her. He kept checking the bump and rocking. It was strange, seeing her smile and cry at once. I suppose she felt both.

qa.q: What did Payal bump her head on?
qa.a: The table.

qa.q: What might Payal have been feeling when she smiled while crying?
qa.a: She probably felt relief at her father's comfort and silly face, mixed with pain from the bump.

qa.q: What did the father do that fits Payal's mixed signals?
qa.a: He kept holding, checking the bump and rocking, following the crying rather than the smile.

qa.q: How does Wasim feel watching Payal smile and cry at once?
qa.a: Wasim finds it strange but thinks she felt both things at the same time.

grounding: A visitor sees a toddler smile and cry at once after a bump, and her father keeps comforting her.

passage:
"Who can name this one?" In the preschool classroom, Vandana, the teacher, held up feeling cards. Karthik named them fast: "Happy! Sad! Angry!" Then she showed a face with wide eyes and an open mouth. "Surprised!" he said.
"Let me tell you what happened just before," Vandana said. "A big dog barked, and the girl ran away."
Karthik looked again, frowning. "Oh. Scared. She's scared."

qa.q: Which faces did Karthik name quickly?
qa.a: Happy, sad and angry.

qa.q: What made Karthik change his answer to "scared"?
qa.a: Hearing what happened just before, the dog barking and the girl running, helped him read the face correctly; he looked thoughtful as he worked it out.

qa.q: What could Vandana keep doing to help children read faces?
qa.a: Tell them what happened just before a face, especially for similar ones like fear and surprise.

qa.q: How might the other children in the class use this?
qa.a: They could learn to ask what happened first before guessing a feeling from a face.

grounding: A preschool teacher helps a child tell fear from surprise by talking about what happened just before the face.

passage: I'm Charu, Minakshi's big sister. We were looking at her picture book, and on one page a girl had wide eyes and her hands up. "She's surprised," Minakshi said. I asked, "What happened on the page before?" She flipped back. Thunder and lightning, and the lights going out. She looked at the girl again. "Scared," she said. "She's scared of the thunder." I don't know if she'd have got it without turning back.

qa.q: What happened on the page before?
qa.a: There was thunder and lightning, and the lights went out.

qa.q: How did Minakshi feel about her new answer?
qa.a: She seemed sure and pleased with herself once she linked the girl's face to the thunder.

qa.q: What did Charu's question teach Minakshi?
qa.a: To look at what happened before a face to understand the feeling.

qa.q: How does Charu see Minakshi's reading of faces?
qa.a: Charu thinks Minakshi needed the story to tell fear from surprise.

grounding: A sister helps a preschooler tell fear from surprise by asking what happened just before.

passage:
Monday: watching a cartoon, Gopika said, "She's surprised," about a girl whose lights had just gone out. Eshaan, her father, asked, "What happened before?" Gopika shrugged.
Wednesday: they paused another cartoon, and Eshaan asked the same question. Gopika thought and said, "A monster came. So... scared?"
The next Monday, she pointed at the screen herself. "She's scared, because the lights went out."

qa.q: What did Eshaan ask on Monday?
qa.a: "What happened before?"

qa.q: How did Gopika feel on the next Monday when she explained the girl's face herself?
qa.a: She seemed confident and proud to work out the feeling on her own from what happened before.

qa.q: What habit of Eshaan's helped Gopika?
qa.a: He kept asking what happened before, which taught her to use the story to read faces.

qa.q: What would change if Eshaan had just told her the answer each time?
qa.a: Gopika might not have learned to work out feelings herself.

grounding: Over a week a father helps a preschooler tell fear from surprise by asking what happened just before.

passage:
Monday: Damini played monster, scowling and snarling at her little cousin Himani. Himani burst into tears.
Wednesday: Damini roared, then giggled between roars, and let Himani see her smiling face behind her claws. Himani watched, unsure, then laughed.
Saturday: Himani put on her own scowl, roared at Damini, and fell over giggling.

qa.q: What did Himani do on Saturday?
qa.a: She put on her own scowl, roared at Damini, and fell over giggling.

qa.q: Why did Himani cry on Monday but laugh on Wednesday?
qa.a: On Monday she felt frightened, reading the scowl as real anger; on Wednesday Damini's giggles showed it was pretend, so she felt safe and amused.

qa.q: What did Damini change that made the game work?
qa.a: She let her giggles and smiling face show between roars, so Himani could see it was play.

qa.q: How might Damini feel when Himani roars back?
qa.a: She would likely feel delighted and proud that Himani now joins in the game.

grounding: Over a week an older child learns to let her giggles show during a monster game so her little cousin sees the scowl is pretend.

passage:
The power went out in their building, and the corridor was pitch dark. Sonali grabbed a torch and decided to be a monster, scowling and growling at her friend Noor. But in the dark Noor couldn't see her face properly, only the growl, and she started to cry.
Sonali quickly shone the torch on her own face. She was grinning. "It's me! I'm laughing!" Noor wiped her eyes, then giggled.

qa.q: What did Sonali grab when the power went out?
qa.a: A torch.

qa.q: Why did Noor cry at first?
qa.a: In the dark she couldn't see Sonali's playful face, only heard the growl, so she felt frightened.

qa.q: What did Sonali do that fixed it?
qa.a: She shone the torch on her grinning face so Noor could see it was pretend.

qa.q: What would change if the lights had been on?
qa.a: Noor could have seen Sonali's giggles and playful body, and might have laughed from the start.

grounding: During a power cut a child's pretend monster face frightens her friend until she shows her grin with a torch.

passage:
In the Mumbai colony garden, Tejas crouched in the bushes playing tiger with his cousin Pranav. When a visiting aunty walked past, Tejas leapt out with a snarl and a deep scowl.
"Arre, why so angry, baba?" she asked, stepping back.
Pranav laughed. "He's a tiger, Aunty. Listen." Behind the scowl, Tejas was giggling so hard his tail of rope wobbled.
The aunty laughed and pretended to run.

qa.q: What was Tejas's tail made of?
qa.a: Rope.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling behind his scowl?
qa.a: He was playful and amused, as his giggling showed, not angry.

qa.q: What helped the aunty read the scowl correctly?
qa.a: Pranav pointed out the giggling, the context that showed it was play.

qa.q: How does the aunty first read Tejas's face?
qa.a: She reads it as real anger and steps back.

grounding: A child's posed tiger scowl is misread as anger until his cousin points out the giggles.

passage: I'm Gopika, and Vandana lives next door. On Sunday her mother found a moustache drawn in pen on her baby brother's photo. "Vandana, did you do this?" Vandana pressed her lips together so tightly they disappeared. But her eyes were all crinkled up, and her shoulders were shaking. She said, "No." Her mother just raised her eyebrows. I couldn't tell if Vandana was sorry or secretly proud of her moustache.

qa.q: What was drawn on the baby brother's photo?
qa.a: A moustache, in pen.

qa.q: What might Vandana have been feeling as she pressed her lips together?
qa.a: She was probably amused and a little proud of her joke, trying to hold back a smile; she may also have felt worried about being in trouble.

qa.q: What could Vandana's mother do next?
qa.a: Calmly say what she sees, that Vandana seems to find it funny, and ask her to help clean the photo.

qa.q: How does Vandana's mother read the pressed lips?
qa.a: Her raised eyebrows suggest she can tell Vandana is holding back a smile.

passage:
Monday: Mohit couldn't find his slippers. "Rashmi, have you seen them?" Rashmi pressed her lips tight, eyes dancing. "No."
Wednesday: at dinner she said a rude-sounding word by accident, then clamped her mouth shut, cheeks puffing with a held-in laugh. Mohit bit back his own smile.
The next Monday: she marched up with the slippers. "I hid them!" and burst out laughing. Mohit laughed too.

qa.q: What did Rashmi hide?
qa.a: The slippers Mohit couldn't find.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when she pressed her lips tight on Monday?
qa.a: She was amused and pleased with her trick, trying to hold back a smile because she knew she shouldn't laugh.

qa.q: How could Mohit respond to Rashmi's held-in smiles?
qa.a: Stay light and let her own up, as she did, rather than punishing the leaking smile.

qa.q: What changed by the next Monday?
qa.a: Rashmi felt safe enough to admit the joke and laugh openly with her father.

grounding: Over a week a child presses her lips to hold back smiles after mischief, until she owns up laughing.

passage:
It was seven forty, and they were late for school. Their mother was rushing out of the door when she saw Mehak's shoes. On the wrong feet. Again.
"Who did this?"
Ankita pressed her lips together hard, looking at the floor. But her eyes creased at the corners and a snort escaped.
Their mother, cross and hurried, stopped. Then she laughed too. "Ankita. Swap them. Quickly!"

qa.q: What was wrong with Mehak's shoes?
qa.a: They were on the wrong feet.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling as she pressed her lips together?
qa.a: She was amused by her joke and trying to hide it, knowing it wasn't the time to laugh.

qa.q: What could Ankita do next time the family is in a rush?
qa.a: Save the joke for a calmer time, since it made them later.

qa.q: How does the mother feel when she notices the held-in smile?
qa.a: She is cross and hurried at first, but the leaking smile makes her laugh too.

grounding: Under time pressure, a child presses her lips to hide a smile after a prank, and it leaks through her eyes.
